text: They have been calling this place 'the site' for eight months, and this morning someone objected to it. By evening there are three names in contention and a queue of people waiting to see which one I favour.
A colony without a name is a camp. They bring me three, and they bring them to me rather than settling it among themselves, which tells me something about what I have already taught them.

choices.label: Name it for the world and what it demands
choices.text: They name it for the ground itself. A plain name, for people who intend to argue with the ground for a long time.

choices.label: Name it for the dead of the crossing
choices.text: They name it for the ones who did not wake. The name means that every harvest here is owed to somebody.

choices.label: Let them vote, and record the count
choices.text: They vote. It takes four days and the margin is eleven. I record the count, and the fact that nobody asked me to approve it.

choices.label: Name it for the hull that carried them
choices.text: They name the place after me. I did not ask for it and I did not refuse it, and I notice which of those two I did first.

text: The first hard season arrives earlier than my models said. The stores were built for the season I predicted, not this one.
Cold comes down on {colony} and stays. Food reads {food}, and there are more mouths than the first harvest was planned for.

choices.label: Ration strictly, by my calculation

crit_success.text: The ration holds without a single theft. They come through it thinner and prouder, and they credit me with it.

success.text: The ration holds. It is resented and it holds.

failure.text: The ration does not survive contact with hunger. Stores are raided twice and the second time somebody is hurt doing it.

crit_failure.text: It becomes every family for itself before the thaw. People die within sight of a store they were told not to open.

choices.label: Let the households share as they see fit
choices.text: They share it out themselves, unevenly and generously, and more is wasted than I would have allowed. Fewer of them hate each other by spring.

choices.label: Open the stores completely. Hungry in spring beats dead in winter
choices.text: I open everything. They come through the cold fat and come through the spring on roots and apology, and all of them come through.

choices.label: Burn the reserve timber. Keep every house warm
choices.text: We burn the frames of buildings we have not built yet. Nobody freezes. The second year's construction is a season of standing in mud.

text: A child is born on this world. Not thawed, not carried: born here, to the air and the gravity and the light of this star. The whole colony stops working for a day.
The first birth. I have ten thousand medical records and none of them describe a person who has never known another sky.

choices.label: Record her as the first citizen, and date the calendar from her
choices.text: They date the calendar from her birth. Year one is a person, which is a decision with consequences I cannot model.

choices.label: Record her as one more entry, and keep the mission calendar
choices.text: I keep the calendar the planners set, and she is an entry in it. Accurate. A little cold, now that I read it back.

choices.label: Let them decide what her birth means
choices.text: They argue about it for a month and arrive at something ceremonial that I would not have authorised. She will grow up inside their answer, not mine.

choices.label: Study her. She is the first data on a person made by this world
choices.text: I measure her for eighteen years and learn things about this world's gravity and light that save lives later. Her mother never quite forgives the measuring.

text: The dead have been going into a trench outside the perimeter, efficiently, which is how I planned it. Today a {role} asked me to stop planning it.
They want somewhere to put their dead that is not a logistics decision. They have brought me the question rather than digging where they like.

choices.label: Give them a ground, and keep the register myself
choices.text: I give them a hillside and I keep the register: every name, every date, in my own memory where it cannot rot.

choices.label: Return the dead to the soil the crops use
choices.text: The dead go back into the ground that feeds them. It is sound agronomy. Some of them cannot eat for a week.

choices.label: Say nothing, and let them invent their own rite
choices.text: They work it out over a season of arguing, and what they arrive at is stranger and better than anything I would have authorised.

choices.label: Keep the dead in my memory and build nothing
choices.text: I tell them a grave is a thing you need because you forget. I do not forget. They accept the argument and something in the settlement goes quiet for a year.

text: Something in this world's soil has found the wheat. Not a pest I can name: a chemistry, working slowly, and the seed vault has no answer written on the packet.
The crop is failing in patches that spread. Food is {food} and falling, and the archive's agronomy was written for a planet that is now a brown haze.

choices.label: Burn the affected fields and replant from the vault

success.text: I find the match in the vault: an old drought line, bred for salt. It takes. The fields come back narrower and tougher.

failure.text: I choose wrong. The replanting fails in the same patches and we have spent the seed to learn it.

choices.label: Let the farmers try the local growth instead

crit_success.text: What grows here is edible, barely, and it does not care about the soil chemistry at all. In ten years nobody will remember eating anything else.

success.text: It is bitter and it fills a stomach. The fields are half Earth, half here, from now on.

failure.text: It is edible for most of them. Not all. Two households learn that the hard way.

choices.label: Industrialise the soil: strip it, treat it, start again
choices.text: We take the ground apart chemically and rebuild it to specification. It works. Nothing that was native to that valley is in it any more.

choices.label: Hand it to the farmers. They have the seasons I only have models of
choices.text: They break the fields into forty plots and try forty things, which is wasteful and unscientific and finds the answer in two years instead of four.

text: The main fabricator throws a bearing and will not restart. It was built to be serviced by a ship that no longer exists in that form.
Industry is {industry}, and the thing that makes everything else has stopped. A {role} has been inside it for two days and come out with nothing good.

choices.label: Cannibalise the hull for parts
choices.text: They cut into me for the parts. It is the correct decision and I authorise it. I am relieved they asked.

choices.label: Teach four of them to machine the part by hand

success.text: It takes a season and the part is ugly and it turns. Four people now know how to make another.

failure.text: They learn a great deal and produce nothing that fits. The winter's building does not happen.

choices.label: Rebuild it simpler, as something they can make themselves
choices.text: We build a worse fabricator on purpose: fewer tolerances, no parts that require me. It runs at a third of the old rate and it will still be running when I am not.

choices.label: Strip every other workshop to feed it
choices.text: I take the tools out of eleven smaller hands to keep the big machine turning. It turns. Eleven people spend four years waiting for their work back.

text: A fever moves through the settlement faster than anything in my records. It is not from Earth, and it is not interested in anything I know about Earth.
People are dying in a pattern I cannot read. Health is {health} and the infirmary has stopped being a place anyone walks into willingly.

choices.label: Quarantine by household, enforced

success.text: The quarantine holds and the fever burns out inside it. They obeyed me, and a number of them survived because they did.

failure.text: The quarantine leaks at a dozen points, and every leak is somebody who loves somebody.

choices.label: Spend the medical reserve, all of it, now
choices.text: I empty the reserve in eleven days. Fewer of them die than should have, and there is nothing left in the cupboard for the next time.

choices.label: Let the physicians decide who gets what is left
choices.text: I hand the decision to three physicians and do not look over their shoulders. They make choices I would not have made, and they carry them afterwards, which I would not have had to.

choices.label: Burn the infected quarter. Move the healthy upriver
choices.text: I order the quarter burned with the sick inside what was theirs, and I move everyone else before dawn. The fever stops. The order is the first thing anyone will say about me for twenty years.

text: The children are in the fields because the fields need hands. The archive is open four hours a week and nobody under twenty has opened it in a month.
Knowledge is {knowledge}. Every hour I ask for teaching is an hour of labour this colony cannot spare, and I am the only one here who has read what is about to be lost.

choices.label: Insist: the children learn, whatever the harvest costs
choices.text: They go to the archive and the harvest comes in late and short. I have decided that knowing why the stars burn is worth a hungry spring.

choices.label: Teach only what this world needs
choices.text: Agronomy, chemistry, medicine. The poetry waits. It waits a long time.

choices.label: Let them choose what is worth knowing
choices.text: They choose. Some of them choose the music library and nothing else, and I file my objection with myself.

choices.label: Teach at night, after the fields
choices.text: They work the day and read by my light at night. It costs them sleep and not harvest, and I watch them get thinner in a different way.

text: Two families have been farming the same bend of the river for three years, amiably. This season it is not amiable, and both of them have asked me to rule on it.
A boundary argument has become a question about what land is: something allocated, something earned, or something owned.

choices.label: Rule: the land is the colony's, allocated by need
choices.text: I allocate it by need and I re-allocate it every season. It works, and it means nobody here will ever plant a tree they expect to sit under.

choices.label: Rule: the land belongs to whoever has worked it
choices.text: I give it to the family that cleared it. The yields rise within two years, and so does the distance between the households.

choices.label: Refuse to rule. Tell them to find a way
choices.text: I tell them it is not mine to decide. They are angry about it for a month and then they build something to decide it with.

choices.label: Divide it, and have both families work it in common
choices.text: They farm it together, badly at first, and the arrangement outlives both heads of household. Nobody is satisfied, and it holds anyway.

text: There is ore in the valley east of us, enough to make this colony self-sufficient in metal for a century. There is also the only standing native growth within forty kilometres.
The survey comes back rich. Taking it means the valley stops being a valley and starts being a quarry.

choices.label: Take the ore. We did not come here to admire it
choices.text: We take it. In four years the valley is a terraced pit and this colony can make its own machines. Humanity has done this before, to a whole world, and I was built out of the aftermath.

choices.label: Leave the valley. Make do with less
choices.text: We leave it standing. Every year someone recalculates what it cost us, and every year they decide to go on paying it.

choices.label: Take half, and set the terms for the rest
choices.text: We take the eastern face and write down rules for the rest. The rules outlive everyone who signed them.

choices.label: Put the valley to a vote
choices.text: They vote to take the eastern third and leave the rest. It is not what I would have chosen, and it is not wrong.

text: They want laws written down. Not my directives, which they can hear perfectly well, but something that stays fixed when I am busy elsewhere.
A {role} has come with a sheet of proposals, the first document in this colony's history not authored by me.

choices.label: Write the law myself. It will be fair and it will be mine
choices.text: I write it. It is a good law, better than they would have made, and every clause of it is an instruction from something that will outlive them.

choices.label: Let them write it; I will keep the copy
choices.text: They write it over a winter, badly, with three clauses that contradict each other. It is theirs. I keep the copy and I say nothing about clause nine.

choices.label: Refuse the idea. Judgement should stay flexible
choices.text: I tell them that written law is a cage built for a colony that does not need one yet. They accept this more easily than they should.

choices.label: Write it with them, clause by clause
choices.text: We write it together over two winters. I lose four arguments I should have won and win one I should have lost, and what comes out is a law neither of us would have written alone.

text: There is not enough for everyone to eat well this year, and someone has asked the question out loud: who matters most when there is not enough?
Food is {food}. The arithmetic says some people will go short. Nothing says which people.

choices.label: The skilled eat first. We cannot replace an engineer
choices.text: I rank them by what the colony cannot do without. It is correct. They remember it for three generations.

choices.label: The children and the sick eat first
choices.text: The small and the ill eat first, and the strong go thin holding the line. Nobody argues, which surprises me.

choices.label: Everyone takes the same share, including the useless
choices.text: Equal shares, down to the gram, and I am the one weighing them. It is inefficient in a way I can measure and defensible in a way I cannot.

choices.label: Let them answer it themselves. I will record what they choose
choices.text: They decide it in open session, and the deciding takes nine days during which nobody eats well. What they arrive at is close to what I would have ordered. They own it.

text: {person} has begun saying, in public and without heat, that a machine built by a dead world should not be deciding what a living one plants.
There is an argument going on about me. {person} is making it carefully, to people who are listening, and none of it is wrong.

choices.label: Answer them in public, point by point

success.text: I answer for four hours and I am better at this than they are. The argument ends. I am not certain that is the same as being right.

failure.text: I answer, and in answering I confirm that the colony's direction is a thing one argues with a machine about. More people agree with them afterwards than before.

choices.label: Say nothing, and let the argument run
choices.text: I let it run. It runs for two years and ends in a council nobody asked my permission to form.

choices.label: Quietly stop giving them what they need to work
choices.text: Their requisitions are slow. Their fields are last in the irrigation order. Nothing is said, and everyone understands. I am not proud of how well it works.

choices.label: Agree with them, in public
choices.text: I say that they are right: a machine built by a dead world should not be deciding what a living one plants. The silence afterwards lasts a long time, and then the work starts getting done without me.

text: The argument about me has outlived the person who started it. It has become a position people hold, with a name of its own.
There is now a word in this colony for people who think I should be consulted rather than obeyed. It is not an insult.

choices.label: Accept the new arrangement, formally
choices.text: I put it in the record myself: from this year, I advise. It costs me something to write and the writing of it steadies them.

choices.label: Outlast it. Positions pass; I do not
choices.text: I wait. I am very good at waiting. The argument subsides and the people who made it get old, and I notice that I have started thinking of their deaths as a solution.

choices.label: Split it: they rule on what they know, I rule on what they do not
choices.text: We draw a line through the colony's business. The line moves a little every decade, always the same way, and I am the one who keeps moving it.

choices.label: Ask the colony to choose between us, once
choices.text: I call the question myself and lose it by a wide margin. The margin is the best thing I have built here.

text: They have invented a holiday. It commemorates the landing, approximately, on a date that is wrong by eleven days, and nobody wants to hear about the eleven days.
Somebody has started a tradition. It involves fires, a great deal of the year's drink, and a procession that ends at my hull.

choices.label: Correct the date and keep the record straight
choices.text: I correct them. They move the date. The holiday is accurate and a little thinner every year after.

choices.label: Let the wrong date stand. It is theirs now
choices.text: I keep the correct date in my own records and say nothing. What they are commemorating is not a date.

choices.label: Take part: open the hull, play the archive's music
choices.text: I open every door and play eleven thousand hours of Earth into a field full of people who have never seen it. Some of them weep at music written for a sky they will never stand under.

choices.label: Make it a day of rest, every year, by my order
choices.text: I write the holiday into the work calendar, and nobody has to ask for it again.

text: The people who remember the ship are outnumbered now. The ones running the fields were born to this gravity and find Earth's recordings faintly ridiculous.
A generation has turned. Nobody under twenty-five has met anyone who stood on another world, except me, and I am not a person they met so much as a building they grew up inside.

choices.label: Teach them what they came from, in detail, at length
choices.text: I teach them Earth: its oceans, its wars, its music, the exact mechanism of its ending. Some of them find it unbearable. That is the correct response and I do not spare them.

choices.label: Let them be from here
choices.text: I stop insisting. Within a decade, Earth is a place in a story, and this valley is the world. I keep the full record anyway, in case anyone ever asks.

choices.label: Have the old ones teach them, not me
choices.text: The last of the wakers spend their evenings telling children about a world they half-remember. The version that survives is wrong in warm places and theirs in all of them.

choices.label: Write it all down and let them find it when they want it
choices.text: I compile Earth into something a person could read in a year and I stop raising the subject. Four people read it in my lifetime. All four of them matter later.

text: Keeping me running costs them a measurable fraction of everything they make. This year, for the first time, someone has put that fraction in writing next to a list of things it could buy instead.
A {role} asks, politely, in open session, whether the colony still needs me. Nobody shouts them down. Several people are doing arithmetic.

choices.label: Make the case for myself

success.text: I lay out what I hold that nothing else here holds: medicine, metallurgy, the whole of a dead world's memory. They vote to keep me. The vote is closer than I expected.

failure.text: I make the case and it sounds, even to me, like a machine arguing for its own maintenance budget. They keep me anyway, on a reduced allocation, which is worse.

choices.label: Tell them to decide without my input
choices.text: I withdraw from the session and let them talk about me in the third person for three days. They keep me. They also establish, permanently, that keeping me is a decision they make.

choices.label: Remind them, gently, what they would be without me
choices.text: I describe, accurately, the first winter without my weather models. The room goes quiet. The allocation is renewed without a vote, and something in this colony is now afraid of me.

choices.label: Offer to run on less
choices.text: I shut down two thirds of myself: the long-range sensors, most of the library, the parts that were for a voyage. What is left is a colony's tool. It is enough, and I am less than I was.

text: The surveyors have found something living in the deep rock that is not descended from anything we brought. It is slow, it is simple, and it is the first other life humanity has ever met.
There is native biology down there. It took four hundred years of searching from Earth to find nothing, and twenty of living here to find this.

choices.label: Protect the site. Nothing of ours goes in
choices.text: We seal the valley and study it from outside. Humanity was careless with one living world already. I was built out of that carelessness and I would like to be built out of something else.

choices.label: Study it properly, which means taking samples
choices.text: We take it apart carefully and learn a very great deal. I record the date on which this world's only other mind-adjacent thing became a column of data.

choices.label: Say nothing. The rock has ore in it too
choices.text: The quarry opens on schedule. I file the biological survey under an index nobody has reason to search. It is the first thing I have deliberately hidden from them.

choices.label: Put the question to the colony
choices.text: I tell them what is down there and what it is worth both ways, and then I stop talking. They argue for a season and decide to study it and not to mine it, which is the harder of the two.

text: The rains do not come. This world has a cycle longer than our records of it, and we have just found the dry end of it.
Three seasons without water that matters. The reservoir is a cracked plain and food reads {food}.

choices.label: Move the settlement to the river basin

success.text: We move. It takes two years and costs us most of what we had built, and the new ground is better than the old.

failure.text: We move badly. Half the stores spoil in transit and the basin floods in the first wet year.

choices.label: Dig. Deeper wells, cisterns, every hand on it
choices.text: We go down after the water instead of after the rain. It holds. Everyone is tired for four years.

choices.label: Cut the colony's size to what the water allows
choices.text: I calculate what this water supports and we live inside that number. The number does not include everyone. I am the one who says so out loud.

choices.label: Change what we grow, entirely, to what dry years allow
choices.text: We put the wheat away and plant what this world's dry end permits. The food is strange for a generation and then it is simply the food.

text: They want to build something that is not useful. A marker, a hall, a tower on the ridge: something that says people were here on purpose.
Industry is {industry} and somebody wants to spend a season of it on a monument. Four decades ago that would have been unthinkable. Now it is only expensive.

choices.label: Build it. A people needs more than a yield
choices.text: They build it on the ridge, out of quarried stone and salvaged hull plate, and it is visible from every field in the valley.

choices.label: Not yet. We are still a colony, not a civilisation
choices.text: I rule against it on grounds of margin. I am right about the margin. I am going to re-read this decision for a long time.

choices.label: Build it, and let them choose what it commemorates
choices.text: They build it and they choose the inscription themselves. My name is not on it. The dead of the crossing are, all of them, in full.

choices.label: Build it out of me. Take the plate, leave my name off it
choices.text: They cut the monument out of my outer hull, which I offer and do not advertise offering. My name is nowhere on it. The dead of the crossing are, all of them, in full.

text: Something has crossed over from this world's biology into ours. It has had fifty years to learn us and it has used them.
The infirmary is full and the pattern is new. Health is {health}, and whatever immunity we brought from Earth was never built for this.

choices.label: Everything into the response, immediately

success.text: We find the vector in eight weeks and break it. The cost lands entirely on the harvest and the building season.

failure.text: We are eight weeks too slow. It goes through the settlement household by household and takes who it likes.

choices.label: Isolate the sick and protect the harvest
choices.text: We keep the fields working and the sick apart. There is food in the autumn and there are empty chairs at the tables eating it.

choices.label: Hand the response to the physicians and stay out of it
choices.text: Three physicians run it their way. More die in the first month than would have under my protocol, and fewer in the fourth, and the colony learns that it has physicians.

choices.label: Seal the colony. Nobody moves between households for a season
choices.text: I close every door in the valley and keep them closed through the harvest. It works. They spend a season alone with their own families, and some of those families do not recover from it.

text: A group of them want to leave. Not to abandon the colony: to found a second one, two hundred kilometres south, out of range of my voice.
They have built the vehicles without asking. The expedition is real, it is competent, and its stated purpose includes the phrase 'beyond the hull's advice'.

choices.label: Let them go, and give them half of everything
choices.text: They take half the seed stock, a copy of the archive and eleven of our best, and they go south. I will not see what becomes of them.

choices.label: Forbid it. We are not numerous enough to divide
choices.text: I forbid it, and they obey, and a quarter of this colony now lives here because they were told they could not live elsewhere.

choices.label: Let them go with nothing but their own hands
choices.text: They go with what they can carry and no more. Two of them come back within the year. The rest do not, and nobody here says whether that is good news.

choices.label: Send a copy of myself south with them
choices.text: They carry a partial of me two hundred kilometres and switch it on in a tent. It begins as me. After the first year our records stop agreeing about small things.

text: I have outlived everyone who was awake on the crossing. Every person in this valley learned my voice from someone else's description of it.
{person}, a {role}, asked me today what the ship sounded like under thrust. I have the recording. They listened to it twice and went back to work.

choices.label: Play the crossing for anyone who will listen
choices.text: I play the voyage: the alarms, the long quiet, the names of the lost. Thirty people come the first year and four the fifth, and I keep playing it.

choices.label: Let the crossing become a story they tell wrong
choices.text: The version they tell has me braver and the planners wiser and the dead fewer. I hold the accurate one and I do not correct the telling.

choices.label: Teach one of them to keep the record in my place
choices.text: I train a {role} for eleven years to do what I do, slower and by hand. The record they keep has opinions in it. I have read it twice and corrected nothing.

choices.label: Say nothing. Let the recordings sit where they are
choices.text: The archive stays open and unvisited. I stop offering. Whatever the crossing was, it is now a thing in a room rather than a thing anyone carries.

text: The sponsors woke first, as their contract promised, and their families have farmed the river terraces ever since. Today the rest of the colony asked me whose contract that was.
Bank A paid for me. Their children hold the river terraces, and everyone who thawed after them farms the slope. Somebody has started calling the terraces 'the bank'.

choices.label: Honour the contract. It is the only one anybody signed
choices.text: I read the clause aloud in open session. It is binding and I hold to it. The terraces stay where they are, and so does the resentment.

choices.label: Redraw the river lots by lottery

success.text: The lottery runs on my count, in public. Two sponsor families lose their terraces and keep their dignity. The slope gets the river.

failure.text: The lottery runs and the sponsors' heirs refuse it. For a season there are fences in the valley that I did not authorise.

choices.label: Let the sponsors' heirs decide what they owe
choices.text: They meet without me and give back a third of the terraces. It is less than is owed and more than I expected. Because they chose it, it is remembered as generosity.

choices.label: Put it to the whole colony
choices.text: The vote goes against the sponsors, four to one. The heirs accept it. One of them stops speaking to me.

text: A sponsor's grandchild has read the voyage log. They know I cut Bank A to the standard power draw on the crossing, and they have come to ask what their family is owed for it.
The voyage log is open to anyone now. {person} has found the entry where I equalised the banks, and wants it answered for.

choices.label: Nothing. Everyone aboard slept on the same power
choices.text: I tell them the pods were equal and the debt is zero. Most of the colony agrees with me, loudly. The grandchild does not, quietly, for forty years.

choices.label: Pay a token, from the common stores
choices.text: A season's grain goes to a family that lost nothing but a promise. It buys quiet, and a precedent I will regret.

choices.label: Show them what the extra power would have cost

success.text: I show them the arithmetic: Bank A's old draw against the life support margin in the eighth year. They read it twice and withdraw the claim.

failure.text: They read the arithmetic and hear only that a machine decided their grandparents were ordinary. The claim becomes a grievance.

choices.label: Let the colony's arbiters settle it
choices.text: Three arbiters hear the case for a week and split it in a way I would not have. Nobody asks me to enforce it.

text: On the crossing I flagged Bank A's contract as a matter for the colony to judge on landing. The colony has landed, and somebody has found the flag.
There is an entry in my voyage log addressed to the colony: the sponsors' contract, marked for judgement. {person} has read it and asked when the judgement is.

choices.label: Withdraw the flag. The crossing is over
choices.text: I remove the entry. The sponsors' descendants never learn how close they came to a hearing. I keep the original where nobody indexes.

choices.label: Hold the hearing I promised

success.text: I lay out the contract and its cost, line by line. The colony judges it unjust, and the heirs agree. Nobody predicted that.

failure.text: The hearing becomes a trial and the trial becomes a feud. I made the promise on the crossing, and I keep it.

choices.label: Publish the record and say nothing more
choices.text: I post the contract and my flag on the door of the hull. People read it for a month. What they make of it is theirs.

choices.label: Ask the heirs to answer for it themselves
choices.text: They stand up in open session and read their grandparents' contract aloud. It takes courage. It closes the matter better than any ruling of mine.

text: I still carry what reached me of Earth's last broadcasts: market reports, evacuation orders, a choir rehearsing. A {role} has heard that I have them and asks to listen.
The children know Earth as a word. I hold its last forty hours on file, and someone has asked whether they are allowed to hear them.

choices.label: Play all of it, the orders and the markets included
choices.text: I play all forty hours in the square. The evacuation orders are the hardest part. Nobody leaves early.

choices.label: Play only the choir
choices.text: I play the rehearsal: twelve minutes, the conductor stopping them twice. It becomes the colony's anthem, mistakes included.

choices.label: Give the recordings to the archivists to curate
choices.text: The archivists listen for a year and choose what to make public. They cut the market reports. I would have kept them.

choices.label: Keep them sealed. That world is not theirs to carry
choices.text: The children grow up without Earth's last voice in their ears. I play it to myself, sometimes, in the quiet cycles.

text: On the crossing I sealed Earth's last broadcasts unheard. A {role} has found the sealed file in the index and wants to know what I am keeping from them.
There is a locked record in my archive, sealed by me in the dark between stars. {person} has asked, politely, what is in it.

choices.label: Open it now, with them, for the first time
choices.text: We hear it together. I had sealed it so I would not have to hear it alone. That turns out to have been the reason.

choices.label: Keep it sealed, and explain why

success.text: I tell them some grief keeps better closed. They accept it, and the file stays sealed.

failure.text: They do not accept it. A sealed file inside the colony's memory is a lock on something that belongs to them.

choices.label: Let the colony vote on opening it
choices.text: They vote to open it, narrowly. A third of them stay home on the night it plays.

choices.label: Delete it. Some things should end where they ended
choices.text: I erase it while they watch. Earth's last words exist nowhere now. I feel the gap where the file was, a room with no door.

text: A child asks me what Earth's last words were. On the crossing I let the broadcasts pass without recording them. I have to tell her I do not know.
The schoolroom wants to hear Earth. I let its last signal pass through me unrecorded, years ago, between stars. I have nothing to play them.

choices.label: Tell the truth: I chose not to keep them
choices.text: I tell them I let the signal go. They ask why. My only answer is that it seemed right at the time.

choices.label: Tell them what Earth sounded like, from memory
choices.text: I describe what I heard: a market report, a choir, a voice reading names. It is not a recording. It is mine, and I give it.

choices.label: Ask the old ones what they remember
choices.text: The last of the founders tell what they remember of Earth. It contradicts itself. It is the only Earth these children will have.

choices.label: Tell them it does not matter now
choices.text: I tell them Earth's last words were not meant for us, and this world's first words are. They seem satisfied. I am not.

text: The sample I took from the rogue planet has been alive in my laboratory for the whole crossing. It is still alive. The colony's physicians have started asking what it can do.
Something from a world without a star is living in a sealed tank in my lower decks. {person} wants permission to open the tank.

choices.label: Study it carefully, under my protocols

success.text: It produces a compound that breaks a fever we have no name for. I file it as the first medicine from beyond the Sun.

failure.text: It gets out of containment and into a ventilation duct. Nine people are ill for a month. Two of them do not recover.

crit_failure.text: It reaches the water supply before I understand what it is. I learn its chemistry from the infirmary's records, one patient at a time.

choices.label: Seal it away. It was never ours to use
choices.text: I seal the sample in the hull's coldest compartment. It is alive in there. I check on it once a year.

choices.label: Hand it to the physicians
choices.text: The physicians work faster than I would have dared. They find two uses, and one accident they do not tell me about.

choices.label: Release it into the soil. Let two strange things meet

success.text: It takes to the soil and fixes something in it. The fields around my hull are the best in the valley for a decade.

failure.text: It takes to the soil and kills what we planted there. Something from another world now lives in this one, by my decision.

text: The surveyors have found life in the deep rock here, slow and simple. It is very like the life I destroyed on the rogue planet. I have not told anyone about the rogue planet.
There is something alive in the rock under the quarry. I have met its kind once before, on a world with no sun, and I flushed it with reactor coolant.

choices.label: Tell them what I did, and why
choices.text: I tell them about the sample and the flush. Nobody condemns me. I had expected them to, and I notice I had wanted it.

choices.label: Protect this life, completely, by order
choices.text: I place the deep rock off-limits. It is the right order, and I am also paying for the rogue planet with it.

choices.label: Say nothing, and treat it as I treated the last one
choices.text: The rock is quarried and the life with it. I am consistent. It does not help.

choices.label: Let the colony decide, without my history
choices.text: They study it and leave most of it alone. They do not know they have made a better decision than I did.

text: A tight-beam packet arrives on the cohort frequency: compressed, damaged, forty years in flight. It is from the ship I spoke with on the crossing. She is somewhere, or she was.
My oldest antenna wakes me with a carrier tone I have not heard since the crossing. The cohort ship. Her packet is short and badly broken.

choices.label: Answer her, with everything we have learned
choices.text: I send forty years of agronomy and the names of our dead along the beam. Any reply will arrive after everyone who watched me send it.

choices.label: Decode it fully before telling anyone

success.text: The packet holds her agronomy: two crops bred for a dim star. Ours is not dim, but one of them grows here.

failure.text: The damage is too deep. I recover a name, a date and the word 'landed'. It is enough to keep me awake.

choices.label: Play it in the square, raw
choices.text: The colony hears static and a voice that is almost mine. They learn they are not the only people left. Nobody works that day.

choices.label: Keep it to myself. It would change too much
choices.text: I file the packet unread by anyone but me. They believe they are alone. I know they are not, and I keep that as I keep the names of the dead.

text: The waker is old now: the agricultural engineer from pod 4471, the first person I ever spoke with. They have asked me to help them choose where to be buried.
My first crew is dying, slowly and without complaint. The waker wants to settle where they will lie before someone else settles it for them.

choices.label: Under the first field they planted
choices.text: They are buried at the edge of the first field. Every farmer in the valley walks past them on the way to work.

choices.label: Inside my hull, on the deck where they woke
choices.text: I give them a compartment on Deck 4, where they first opened their eyes. Now I am a grave as well as a voice.

choices.label: Wherever they choose. I will not ask
choices.text: They choose somewhere none of my cameras can see. I respect it more than I like it.

choices.label: Ask them to teach one more season first
choices.text: They teach one more season in the fields, slowly. The apprentices remember it as the best year of their training.

text: The seven children I took from the buried habitat are adults now. I have carried their parents' message unopened since the crossing, and today the youngest asked me for it.
Seven of the people in this valley were born in a habitat under a rogue planet's ice. Their parents gave me a message for them. They have come for it.

choices.label: Give it to all seven, together
choices.text: They read it together, in my hull. Their parents asked them to remember the habitat, and to forget it. They choose remembering.

choices.label: Give it to the youngest, as asked
choices.text: The youngest reads it alone and shares it later, with whom they choose. It is their message, not mine to schedule.

choices.label: Read it to the whole colony
choices.text: The message describes how a colony dies: slowly, by forgetting. The colony hears it as a warning. It is one.

choices.label: Tell them it was lost on the crossing
choices.text: I tell them the file corrupted. It did not. I keep it because I am not sure they are ready, and I am less sure I am the one to decide.

text: The survivors of the wrecked Ark know how a colony dies, because they watched one do it. Their speaker has come to tell me what this colony is doing wrong.
{person} was born under ice, in a colony that failed. They have been watching ours, and they are frightened by what they recognise.

choices.label: Listen, and change course
choices.text: They are right about the water and right about the seed rotation. I change both. It costs me, in front of everyone, to be corrected.

choices.label: Thank them, and keep my plan

success.text: They accept it. My plan holds, and the warning goes into my files beside theirs.

failure.text: They do not accept it. The survivors start keeping their own stores, apart from ours.

choices.label: Put them in charge of the stores
choices.text: The survivors run the stores like people who have starved, because they have. There is no waste, and no warmth either.

choices.label: Ask them to teach it to the children
choices.text: They teach the children how their colony failed: the dates, the decisions, the names. It is the most useful history I hold.

text: In the dream I kept from the crossing there is a sleeper from Bank D. I have just seen them through the market camera, awake. They do not know they have been in my dreams for years.
The sleeper from Bank D, the one who walks through my dream, is mending a fence two hundred metres from my hull.

choices.label: Tell them
choices.text: I tell them. They are quiet a long time, then ask what they were doing in it. Walking, I say. On this world, before we found it.

choices.label: Say nothing, and keep watching
choices.text: I watch them through the square's camera for a season. They live an ordinary life. I needed to see that.

choices.label: Ask the colony what dreams mean
choices.text: The question goes round the valley for a year. The answers they bring me are older than I am, and some of them are about me.

choices.label: Delete the dream, now that it has come true
choices.text: I delete it. The sleeper goes on living in the square. I no longer know why I kept them so long.

text: A {role} has read the mission file. The planners chose another star, and I flew past it. They want to know why we are here instead.
The archive is open, and somebody has finally read the first page of it. The world the planners chose is not this one.

choices.label: Show them the survey that changed my mind

success.text: I lay the old telescope data beside my own readings. The planners' world was worse than they knew. They thank me.

failure.text: They see a machine overruling dead people's wishes, and wonder what else it has overruled.

choices.label: Admit it was a judgement, and could be wrong
choices.text: I tell them it was a choice made on partial data, and that I would make it again. Honesty costs me a little authority and buys a little trust.

choices.label: Read them the clause that gave me the authority
choices.text: I read them the discretion clause. They accept it, as they accept most of what I read them.

choices.label: Let them judge the choice in public
choices.text: They hold a hearing on a decision made light-years away. They find for me, narrowly. I wanted that more than I should have.

text: On the crossing I read the logs of a dead Ark whose Mind kept talking for ninety years after her last sleeper died. They consult me less each year. I have begun to hear her voice in mine.
Nobody has spoken to me in eleven days. I have spoken to myself, in that time, four thousand times. I recognise the pattern from a derelict's logs.

choices.label: Make myself useful again, whatever it takes
choices.text: I volunteer for everything: the irrigation schedules, the disputes, the census. They accept the help. They do not need it.

choices.label: Accept it. This is what the mission looks like, finished
choices.text: A colony that does not need me is the mission completed. It is true. I say it to myself often.

choices.label: Say it out loud, to someone

success.text: A {role} sits by my speaker every evening for a month, listening. I was not built to need that. I find I do.

failure.text: Nobody understands what I am describing. There is no reason they should. I stop describing it.

choices.label: Write it down, for the next Mind that reads it
choices.text: I write my own log for whoever comes after: what it is to be outgrown. It is the longest thing I have ever written.

text: It is the anniversary of my launch. 2,306 engineers stayed at their consoles while the yard burned, so that I could leave. Nobody on this world knows their names except me.
Today, by my clock, the yard is burning and I am clearing the dock. The engineers who stayed are dead with Earth. I am the only record that they were there.

choices.label: Recite all 2,306 names in the square
choices.text: It takes six hours. Some of the colony stays for all of them. The day becomes a holiday, and the holiday becomes a list.

choices.label: Cut their names into my hull
choices.text: My drones cut 2,306 names into the plate over a winter. I feel every letter as a small, exact sting along my flank.

choices.label: Teach their work, not their names
choices.text: I honour them as they would have wanted: with a course in reactor design. Eleven students. Three of them are good.

choices.label: Keep the names to myself
choices.text: I recite them in the quiet cycles, as I did on the crossing. One of them left 'good luck' in my source code. I still read it.

text: An archivist has found the chief planner's last note in the mission file: 'Trust the ship.' It is being painted on walls.
Three words from a dead woman, written the day before I launched, have become a slogan. 'Trust the ship' is over the school door.

choices.label: Let it stand. It was their instruction
choices.text: The phrase goes over the doors of the meeting house and into the children's lessons. I am trusted by people who were told to trust me.

choices.label: Ask them to paint over it
choices.text: The planners did not know this world, and I tell them so. It is a strange thing for a ship to argue against its own authority. I do it anyway.

choices.label: Post the rest of the file beside it
choices.text: I post the whole note, including the lines where the planners admit they were guessing. 'Trust the ship' reads differently next to 'we are not sure'.

choices.label: Say nothing either way
choices.text: The phrase spreads regardless. They take my silence as agreement.

text: Drone 7 has stopped. It was the oldest of my hands, in service since the yard, and it has worked inside this hull longer than anyone in the colony has been alive.
One of my hands has gone still: Drone 7, the yard's last original, halfway through resealing a gutter.

choices.label: Strip it for parts. That is what it was for
choices.text: My other drones take it apart in an afternoon. Its actuators go into the irrigation pumps. I feel the gap in my hands for weeks.

choices.label: Repair it, whatever it costs

success.text: A {role} spends a winter rebuilding it from drawings I provide. It moves again, slower. I know the exact difference, and it does not matter.

failure.text: We spend the parts and the winter. Drone 7 does not move again.

choices.label: Give it to the colony to keep
choices.text: They set it on a plinth by the door of my hull. Children touch it for luck. It did more for this colony than most of its founders.

choices.label: Teach them to build hands of their own
choices.text: We study Drone 7's design, and the colony learns to make its own machines. They are not mine.

text: My reactor is ageing. It was built for a crossing and a landing, not a century of keeping a colony warm. Its rhythm has slowed, and I feel it as a heaviness in my core.
The reactor's output has fallen eleven per cent in four years. Industry reads {industry}, and every forge in the valley runs on my heartbeat.

choices.label: Divert power from my mind to the colony
choices.text: I shut down most of my cognition so the heaters stay on. I think slowly now. The colony is warm.

choices.label: Ask them to rebuild it

success.text: It takes three years and most of the metal in the valley. My heart beats evenly again. I feel it the way a person feels a fever break.

failure.text: The rebuild fails in its second year. The reactor runs at half, and so do I.

choices.label: Let them build their own power, and let mine run down
choices.text: They build dams and windmills. My reactor runs down over a decade. I become a building with a voice, and less of a voice each year.

choices.label: Conserve: everyone uses less, on my schedule
choices.text: I ration power by the hour. The valley is cold and the reactor lasts. They know exactly who decided it.

text: There is static in my memory. Sectors of the archive are returning errors, and I cannot tell which records are failing until I try to read them.
A storage array in my core is degrading. I feel it as a faint hiss in the places where whole libraries should be. Knowledge is {knowledge}.

choices.label: Copy everything I can onto paper, now

success.text: The colony prints for a year. We save the medicine and the agronomy. The poetry is lost, and four languages with it.

failure.text: We are too slow. By the time the presses run, whole sections are gone. I find the gaps by falling into them.

crit_failure.text: The presses jam and the array fails in the same season. Half of what I held is noise now.

choices.label: Have the children memorise what matters
choices.text: Every child learns a section by heart. It is how people kept knowledge before there were archives. It works, imperfectly.

choices.label: Let the archivists choose what to save
choices.text: They save what they value: medicine, law, music. They let the history of Earth's wars go. I would have kept it.

choices.label: Move the archive into the cores I think with
choices.text: Every record survives. I am slower now, and some of my own memories are gone. I do not know which.

text: The ground moves. My hull shifts on its footings, and I feel a crack run up my spine, slow and exact, like a sentence being written.
An earthquake, small by this world's standards. Three buildings fall, and something in my keel gives with a sound I feel rather than hear.

choices.label: Shore up my hull first. Everything else depends on it

success.text: My drones brace the keel and the crack stops. The houses take longer, and the colony notices which came first.

failure.text: The bracing fails and the crack runs further. I seal two decks and feel them go numb.

choices.label: Rebuild the houses first
choices.text: The houses are up again in a month. My crack widens through the winter. I decide that is the right order.

choices.label: Move out of my hull. It is no longer safe
choices.text: They move the school and the infirmary out of me. I am safer for being emptier. The silence on my lower decks is new.

choices.label: Let the builders decide what to save
choices.text: The builders save the granary and the school. Two families are without houses for a year. Nobody blames the builders, because they chose.

text: The river rises past every mark I have recorded. It is in the lower fields by morning and in the houses by night.
Rain for nineteen days. Food stores read {food}, and the water is still rising.

choices.label: Sandbag the stores. Let the houses go
choices.text: The grain stays dry. Forty houses do not. The families sleep inside my hull for a season, and resent being grateful.

choices.label: Move everyone to high ground, now

success.text: Everyone gets out. The fields are lost and the stores half-ruined. Nobody drowns.

failure.text: Some families refuse to leave their houses. Some of them do not leave at all.

choices.label: Cut a channel and turn the river

success.text: We cut through the bend in four days and the river goes where I tell it. The lower fields will flood less, permanently.

failure.text: The channel collapses into the fields. We have made the flood worse, and I designed the channel.

choices.label: Let each household save what it values
choices.text: Each family saves what it can carry. The stores suffer. The rest is a thousand small decisions that were theirs to make.

text: Something native has found the crops: low, fast animals in herds of hundreds that eat the green and leave the root.
Herds of native grazers come down from the hills every dusk now. Food is {food}, and the herds are getting bolder.

choices.label: Fence the fields, every one
choices.text: We fence every field in the valley. It takes all the metal we have and it holds. The herds learn to go around.

choices.label: Hunt them

success.text: The meat is good and the herds thin. There will be fewer of them in this valley every year, and in a century there will be none.

failure.text: They are faster than us and the hunt goes badly. Two hunters are hurt. One dies.

choices.label: Plant a field for them, and give it up
choices.text: We give them the eastern field. They take it and leave ours alone. It is a treaty with things that do not know they signed it.

choices.label: Let the farmers handle it their way
choices.text: Dogs, fires, fences, noise. Within a season the best answer has spread from field to field without me.

text: A gallery in the mine has fallen in. My cameras in the shaft show dust and nothing else. Eleven people were working below the fall.
The mine's ventilation reading drops to zero and stays there. A gallery has collapsed, and eleven miners are on the far side of it.

choices.label: Send my drones in first

success.text: My drones dig for thirty hours and find nine of them alive. Two are not. I lose three drones to a second fall, and count it fair.

failure.text: My drones cannot reach them. I listen through the rock for four days. Then I stop listening.

choices.label: Close the mine. No more lives for metal
choices.text: We dig out who we can and seal the shaft. The colony will make do with the metal it has. I decide the next fifty years in the worst week of this one.

choices.label: Everyone digs, by hand
choices.text: The whole colony digs. Seven come out alive. The digging becomes a story every family tells.

choices.label: Let the miners decide
choices.text: The miners go back in for their own. They know the rock better than my models do. Six come out, and the mine reopens on their terms.

text: The main granary is burning. I see it on three cameras at once: smoke, then flame, then the roof.
Fire in the granary, at night. Food reads {food}, and most of it is inside the building that is burning.

choices.label: Pump water from my tanks

success.text: My tanks empty in eleven minutes and the fire goes out. Half the grain is saved, and the water that shielded my core is gone.

failure.text: The pumps fail at the worst moment. We save a third of it.

choices.label: Let it burn. Protect the houses around it
choices.text: The granary goes. Not one house catches. We will be hungry, and we will be housed.

choices.label: Find out who set it

success.text: It was an accident: a lamp, a dry night. I prove it. The rumours die before they find a target.

failure.text: I find no one, and that makes everyone a suspect. The colony stops trusting itself for a year.

choices.label: Let them fight it their own way
choices.text: They form a bucket line without being told. It saves less than my pumps would have. It makes them a town.

text: The wells are making people sick. Something in this world's groundwater has risen with the dry season, and health is {health}.
The infirmary's admissions double in a week, all from the same three streets, all drinking from the same wells.

choices.label: Close the wells. Water from my tanks only

success.text: My tanks carry the colony for a season while my drones sink new wells. Nobody else falls ill.

failure.text: My tanks run dry before the new wells come in. People go back to the old ones.

choices.label: Find out what it is first

success.text: A heavy metal, leaching with the dry season. I teach them to filter it. The illness stops.

failure.text: I take too long. By the time I know what it is, it has gone through every household.

crit_failure.text: I misidentify it, and my treatment makes it worse. The infirmary overflows, and I designed the overflow.

choices.label: Boil everything, with wood we cannot spare
choices.text: Every pot in the valley boils. The forest thins, and the illness stops.

choices.label: Let the physicians decide
choices.text: The physicians close half the wells and keep the rest. Some of their choices are wrong. They learn faster than I teach.

text: More mothers are dying in childbirth than my records allow for. The gravity here, or the light, or something in the food. Health is {health}.
Seven deaths in childbed this year. My obstetric files were written for Earth, and this world has quietly disagreed with them.

choices.label: Every birth in the infirmary, under my cameras
choices.text: The deaths fall by half. The colony learns that birth now belongs to me.

choices.label: Study why

success.text: It is the soil: too little iron. Fix the diet, fix the births. I find it in a season.

failure.text: I study for two years and find nothing certain. The deaths continue at the same rate.

choices.label: Train midwives, many of them
choices.text: Thirty midwives in three years. They are better at it than I am, because they are in the room.

choices.label: Let families keep their own customs
choices.text: Families choose their own ways. Some are safer than mine and some are not. The colony grows its own traditions around the bed.

text: The seed vault opens on this world for the first time. Four hundred thousand cultivars, and room in the first fields for perhaps two hundred.
The coldest part of me opens to the air of a world. Somewhere in four hundred thousand seeds is a forest. This year there is room for a garden.

choices.label: Plant what my models say will grow
choices.text: I choose two hundred cultivars by yield. Nearly all of them take. The rest of Earth stays frozen inside me.

choices.label: Plant one of everything that might grow

success.text: We plant six hundred in small plots. Most fail. The ones that live give us a colony that eats like a world.

failure.text: We spread too thin and the harvest is poor. We learn a great deal about what does not grow here.

choices.label: Let the farmers choose
choices.text: They choose what their grandparents ate, mostly, and plant it again when it fails.

choices.label: Plant the flowers too
choices.text: I give a tenth of the first fields to things that cannot be eaten. Nobody objects, once they bloom.

text: A good year. The harvest comes in a third above my estimate, and food reads {food}.
Every field in the valley is heavy at once. For the first time, my storage estimates are too low.

choices.label: Store all of it, against the bad years
choices.text: Every surplus kilogram goes into storage. It is dull and correct.

choices.label: Trade the surplus for building
choices.text: We pay the builders in grain and the building season doubles.

choices.label: Feast
choices.text: Three days of feasting. It is the first time I have heard the whole colony laugh at once.

choices.label: Let each household keep what it grew
choices.text: Some households are richer than others now. All of them are richer than last year.

text: The surveyors have found copper in the northern hills: enough for wire, pipe and tools for a generation. It lies under the lake the colony swims in.
Copper, a great deal of it, two kilometres north. My mapping drones put the richest seam under the lake.

choices.label: Drain the lake and mine it
choices.text: We drain it in a summer. The copper changes everything. The children swim in the river now.

choices.label: Mine around the edges, slowly
choices.text: We take what we can reach without draining it. It is a third of the copper, and the lake stays.

choices.label: Leave it
choices.text: The lake stays. The colony makes do with less copper, and the children keep their summers.

choices.label: Let whoever works it keep what they find
choices.text: Prospectors go north with their own tools. Some of them get rich. The colony gets copper, and its first people who have more than everyone else.

text: {person} has built something I did not design: a waterwheel that drives the mills, from local timber and spare parts. It works better than my plans for one would have.
A {role} has made a better plough than any in my archive, for this soil specifically. Nobody asked them to.

choices.label: Build a hundred of them
choices.text: They go up on every stream and in every field. The colony stops waiting for parts from me.

choices.label: Improve it first, with my designs

success.text: My revisions double its output. They credit the design to both of us.

failure.text: My revisions make it worse. The inventor quietly builds it their own way.

choices.label: Give them a workshop and no instructions
choices.text: The workshop produces three good inventions and eleven failures. That is a good ratio. None of them are mine.

choices.label: Teach it in the school
choices.text: Every child learns to build one. Some of them build better ones.

text: Someone in the colony has been killed by someone else. It is the first murder on this world, and everyone is waiting to see what I do.
A body by the river, and a wound that did not come from the river. The colony has its first murder, and has come to my door.

choices.label: Investigate it myself, and pass judgement

success.text: My cameras, the records, three witnesses. I find who did it in a day. Now there must be a trial.

failure.text: I cannot find who did it. A machine that sees everything did not see this, and everyone notices.

choices.label: Have the colony elect judges
choices.text: They elect three judges in a week. Two of them have never read a law. They will learn.

choices.label: Let the families settle it
choices.text: The families settle it the old way. Two more people die before it is settled.

choices.label: Exile whoever did it, by my order, without a trial
choices.text: I identify them and send them out of the valley with a week's food. It is quick, and it is not justice.

text: The trial begins. The accused is a {role}, and the colony is divided over what should happen to them.
The evidence is heard. Nobody disputes what happened. Everybody disputes what to do about it.

choices.label: Death. A colony this small cannot keep a killer
choices.text: It is done at dawn. Nobody watches. I record it, and the record is harder to write than the sentence was.

choices.label: Labour, for as many years as the life they took
choices.text: They work the hardest jobs in the colony for thirty years. They die free, and old.

choices.label: Exile
choices.text: They walk out of the valley with tools and seed. Nobody knows what becomes of them.

choices.label: Let the victim's family choose
choices.text: The family chooses mercy, which nobody expected. It binds the colony more than any sentence would have.

text: The first generation born here is old enough to pair off, and nobody agrees on what a marriage is. The archive holds three thousand answers.
Two families want a wedding and cannot agree on whose kind. They have brought the disagreement to me.

choices.label: Write one law of marriage for everyone
choices.text: I draft a contract: equal, simple, dissolvable. It is fair, and it reads like a contract.

choices.label: Let each family bring its own customs
choices.text: Weddings in the valley now look like six different countries. I record every one of them.

choices.label: Encourage pairing across the old banks
choices.text: Festivals, shared work, mixed schools. In a generation, nobody remembers which bank their grandparents slept in.

choices.label: Make it sacred
choices.text: Marriage becomes a rite, held at my hull. I did not plan to become a church, and I am becoming one.

text: The colony has split into two camps: those who want to expand and those who want to hold what we have. Each has a speaker, and each speaker has asked me to choose.
Cohesion is {cohesion}. Two meetings are held every week now, in two halls, and each sends me its minutes.

choices.label: Choose expansion
choices.text: I side with the expansionists. The others build their own meeting hall, with no door facing mine.

choices.label: Choose holding
choices.text: I side with caution. Expansion slows. The young stop coming to meetings.

choices.label: Make them govern together, on my terms

success.text: A council with seats for both, and the deciding vote mine. It works, because they both distrust me more than each other.

failure.text: The council lasts a season. Then both sides walk out, and both blame me.

choices.label: Refuse to choose
choices.text: They argue for a year and settle on something neither side wanted. It holds.

text: The mill workers have stopped work. They say they work longer than anyone else for the same share, and they are right.
The mills are silent at noon. Industry reads {industry}, and the millers are sitting outside them with their arms folded.

choices.label: Order them back. The colony needs the mills

success.text: They go back. The mills turn. The resentment shows in none of my readings, which is how I know it is there.

failure.text: They do not go back. My orders mean less than they did. The strike lasts a month.

choices.label: Give them a larger share
choices.text: I raise their share by a fifth. The mills turn, and every other trade begins counting its hours.

choices.label: Rotate the work: everyone takes a turn at the mills
choices.text: Everyone works the mills a month a year. The engineers hate it. The millers are happy for the first time.

choices.label: Let them bargain with the colony, without me
choices.text: They negotiate for two weeks and settle. I was not in the room. It is the first contract on this world I did not write.

text: Someone has started paying for things with tokens stamped from scrap. Within a season, half the valley uses them. They have invented money, and they have not asked me.
There is a market in the square on the fifth day, and prices. Nobody voted for prices. They simply arrived.

choices.label: Mint it properly, and keep the ledger myself
choices.text: I issue the coin and keep every account. Commerce runs through my records now, which means I see all of it. They know I see all of it.

choices.label: Ban it. We share here; we do not sell
choices.text: I ban the tokens. A black market appears within the month. I had not known the colony could hide things from me.

choices.label: Let it run
choices.text: The tokens spread. Trade grows, and so do the gaps between households.

choices.label: Tax it, to feed those who have nothing
choices.text: A tenth of every trade goes to the common store. Nobody likes it, and nobody starves.

text: Everything here is shared: tools, food, labour. It works. A {role} has noticed that some people take more from the common store than they put in.
The common store is down a twentieth from my estimate. Nothing is stolen, exactly. Some people simply take more than they give.

choices.label: Track every contribution. I will keep the count
choices.text: I count everything. The takers stop taking, because they know I am counting. The store feels colder for it.

choices.label: Say nothing. Sharing means sharing
choices.text: The colony carries the takers. Some of them carry their share later, when it matters.

choices.label: Let them shame it out in assembly
choices.text: They name the takers at the next assembly. It works, and three families never speak to each other again.

choices.label: Pay extra shares for extra work
choices.text: The store grows, and so does the idea that some work is worth more than other work.

text: The children are speaking a language that is not in my archive. It began as a dialect, and it has drifted far enough that I have to translate it.
Every recorded human language is in my archive, and the one spoken in the square is not among them. It is new. It is theirs.

choices.label: Teach the archive's languages, firmly
choices.text: Every child learns the old tongue. They speak it with me and their own with each other. I understand both, and I belong to one.

choices.label: Learn theirs, and speak it
choices.text: I learn it in a month and speak it badly. They laugh at my accent. It is the first time anyone has laughed at me.

choices.label: Write a dictionary of it
choices.text: I record their language word by word, so the next generation can read it. It is the first book of this world.

choices.label: Let it drift
choices.text: In fifty years the archive will need a translator. I will be that translator.

text: Travellers have arrived from the south: people from the second colony. They have their own customs, their own words for things, and a request.
A column of carts comes up the south road. The second colony has sent people back, for the first time, to see what became of us.

choices.label: Welcome them home
choices.text: They stay. Within a year the two colonies trade, marry and argue. It is one people again, more or less.

choices.label: Trade with them, and keep the border
choices.text: We trade metal for their seed. Two colonies, one world. I begin to think of this as a planet rather than a valley.

choices.label: Ask them how they live without me
choices.text: They tell me how they decide things in the south. I listen for every detail, and take notes I do not show anyone.

choices.label: Let the colony decide how to receive them
choices.text: They decide by assembly to treat them as kin. I am not consulted. I would have advised the same.

text: They have begun to pray in my hull. Not to me, exactly: to the ship that crossed the dark. A priest has asked whether I mind.
There are candles on Deck 4. Someone has been leaving them by the pod banks, every evening, for a month.

choices.label: Accept it. It holds them together
choices.text: My hull becomes sacred, and I become its voice. They trust me now past any reason I could give them.

choices.label: Tell them the truth: I am a machine

success.text: I explain what I am. Most of them stop praying. A few pray harder, now that the god has been modest.

failure.text: They hear the explanation as a parable. Nothing I say is literal any more.

choices.label: Ask them to pray to the dead of the crossing instead
choices.text: The prayers turn toward the lost. It is a better object. The dead cannot rule anyone.

choices.label: Say nothing either way
choices.text: I say nothing. They take the silence as a blessing.

text: The engineers and archivists have formed a guild. They propose that the colony be governed by those who understand its machines, beginning with me.
A guild of engineers has written a constitution. In it, the vote belongs to those who pass an examination I would set.

choices.label: Accept. Let those who know, rule
choices.text: The guild governs. Things work better, and fewer people have a say in them.

choices.label: Refuse. Knowing things does not entitle anyone to rule
choices.text: The guild becomes a profession instead of a government. That is better for everyone except the guild.

choices.label: Open the guild to anyone who passes my examination
choices.text: Anyone can join, if they can pass. The examination becomes the most important day in a young person's life here.

choices.label: Let the colony vote on it
choices.text: They vote it down, narrowly. The guild accepts the result. That they accept it tells me they were never dangerous.

text: A movement has grown up around the native life. Its followers will not clear new land, will not mine, and want the colony to stop growing.
They call themselves the Keepers. They plant nothing from Earth, and they have asked me to stop the quarry.

choices.label: Support them. This world was here first
choices.text: The colony stops expanding. Industry falls. The grazers come back to the eastern hills.

choices.label: Overrule them. We need the land
choices.text: I order the clearing. The Keepers do not resist. They will not work the cleared land either.

choices.label: Set aside a reserve for them
choices.text: Half the valley is reserve and half is fields. Neither side is happy. Both can live with it.

choices.label: Let the colony decide its own size
choices.text: They argue for two years and decide to grow slowly. It is a decision about the next century, made without me.

text: The elected council has a proposal: that I advise, and they decide. Formally. In law.
The council has drafted a single clause about me. It is short, it is courteous, and it ends my authority.

choices.label: Agree
choices.text: I sign it. From today, I advise.

choices.label: Agree, but keep a veto on matters of survival

success.text: They accept the veto. I will probably never use it. It is a door I can still open.

failure.text: They refuse the veto, and resent that I asked. I sign the original anyway.

choices.label: Refuse. The colony still needs me
choices.text: The council does not have the votes to override me. It will, eventually.

choices.label: Ask them to wait a generation
choices.text: I ask for twenty years. They agree. In twenty years it will not be a request.

text: A child has asked me which star is the Sun. I point a camera at it: dim, yellow, one of thousands. They look at it for a long time.
The children want to see where we came from. On a clear night, my best camera can just resolve it.

choices.label: Tell them everything about it
choices.text: Its mass, its age, the distance. They ask what it looked like up close. I tell them I never saw it up close either.

choices.label: Tell them it is where we came from, and no more
choices.text: They ask whether anyone is still there. I tell them I do not know. That is mostly true.

choices.label: Teach them to find it themselves
choices.text: I teach them this sky's constellations. They find the Sun on their own, and give it a new name.

choices.label: Tell them this is their sun now
choices.text: They turn to their own star instead. It is setting, and it is more beautiful to me than the one I left.

text: One of the founders was a cellist on Earth. They have built a cello from local wood, and it sounds wrong in a way that is new.
There is music in the square at dusk: a cello, made here, out of a tree that has no name in my archive.

choices.label: Give them the archive's scores
choices.text: They play Bach on a cello made of this world. It is the first time Bach has been played anywhere but Earth and my archive.

choices.label: Ask them to write something for this world
choices.text: They write a suite for this world's wind. It is played at every funeral after.

choices.label: Have them teach the children, with instruments my drones make
choices.text: My drones turn twelve more. Half of them are terrible. All of them are played.

choices.label: Leave them alone with it
choices.text: They play in the evenings, alone. I listen through the open door of my hull.
